info:
Unlike English, where letters are written linearly (left to right), Korean letters are arranged in a 2D square block to represent a single syllable.

Each syllable has:

Initial consonant (top or left)

Vowel (right or below)

Optional final consonant (bottom)

2. Letters shift shape or orientation to fit the syllable layout
Some vowels change orientation depending on the type of vowel:

Horizontal vowels:
ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ

These go under the consonant.

Example:

고 = ㄱ + ㅗ

구 = ㄱ + ㅜ

👉 Vertical vowels:
ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅣ

These go to the right of the consonant.

Example:

가 = ㄱ + ㅏ

거 = ㄱ + ㅓ

This causes the same letter (ㄱ) to appear in different positions and with different spacing depending on the vowel.

3. Visual balance drives shape changes
Some parts of letters may appear slightly stretched, compressed, or shifted to keep the syllable block visually square and balanced.

For example:

In 밥 (ㅂ + ㅏ + ㅂ), the second ㅂ at the bottom is smaller and centered.
